# Trends in Discharge Rates for Acute Pulmonary Embolism in US Emergency Departments

**Authors:** Nathan W. Watson; Brett J. Carroll; Anna Krawisz; Alec Schmaier; Eric A. Secemsky

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 2Smith Center for Outcomes Research in Cardiology, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA | 3Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA

## Abstract

Outpatient management for selected patients with low-risk acute pulmonary embolism (PE) has been proven safe and effective, yet recent evidence suggests that patients are still managed with hospital admission. Few studies have assessed the contemporary real-world trends in discharge rates for acute PE from US emergency departments (ED).

To evaluate if the proportion of discharges from the ED for acute PE have changed between 2012–2020 and which baseline characteristics are associated with ED discharge.

Serial cross-sectional analysis.

US EDs participating in the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey.

ED visits for acute PE between 2012–2020.

None

National trends in the proportion of discharges for acute PE; factors associated with ED discharge.

Between 2012–2020, there was an estimated total of 1,635,300 visits for acute PE. Overall, ED discharge rates remained constant over time from 38.2% (95% CI, 17.9%–64.0%) between 2012–2014 to 33.4% (95% CI, 21.0%–49.0%) between 2018–2020 (adjusted risk ratio, 1.01 per year; 95% CI, 0.89–1.14). No baseline characteristics, including established risk stratification scores, were predictive of an increased likelihood of ED discharge; however, patients at teaching hospitals and with private insurance were more likely to receive oral anticoagulation at discharge. Only 35.9% (95% CI, 23.9%–50.0%) of patients considered low-risk by PESI class, 33.1% (95% CI, 21.7%–47.0%) by sPESI score, and 34.8% (95% CI, 23.3%–48.0%) by hemodynamic stability were discharged from the ED setting.

Cross-sectional survey design, inability to adjudicate diagnoses.

In a representative nationwide sample, rates of discharge from the ED for acute PE appear to have remained constant over the past nine years. Only one-third of low-risk patients were discharged for outpatient management and rates appear to have stabilized. We speculate that outpatient management for low-risk acute PE is still largely underutilized in the US.

None

## INTRODUCTION

Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is one of the leading causes of cardiovascular-related mortality and is responsible for nearly 300,000 deaths annually (1,2). As a result, clinical management for patients with acute PE often necessitates inpatient hospital admission for anticoagulation or other advanced therapies (3,4). However, in recent years, it has become increasingly clear that outpatient management for selected, low-risk patients with acute PE is a safe and feasible approach (5–7). To date, multiple randomized controlled trials have been completed and have collectively demonstrated that outpatient management among select patients is associated with low rates of recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, and mortality when compared to hospitalization (8,9). These findings have resulted in changes in international guidelines published by various clinical societies including the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and CHEST (10,11). Adoption of these guidelines has the potential to improve patient care and also substantially reduce overall healthcare spending by limiting costly inpatient admissions (12,13).

Despite this increasing evidence, recent work has suggested that many patients with low-risk PE are still managed with inpatient hospitalization (14–16). For example, in a limited analysis among community health systems, nearly 85% of patients with low-risk PE were hospitalized despite updates to clinical practice guidelines (17). This observation is particularly important as US health care costs continue to surge and overcrowding within EDs remain to be a critical issue (18,19). While previous work has demonstrated an increase in outpatient utilization for acute PE, few contemporary studies have focused specifically on this decision-making process within the emergency department (ED), a frequent location for these triage decisions (20,21). Additionally, little is known regarding the national patterns in discharge rates for acute PE within the United States. As the landscape of PE management continues to rapidly evolve and immediate oral anticoagulation with direct oral anticoagulants has now been firmly established as first-line therapy, understanding the national management patterns is of critical importance.

In this study, we utilized a nationally representative dataset to assess the recent real-world, national trends in discharge rates for acute PE from United States EDs. We specifically sought to (1) evaluate if the proportion of discharges for low-risk acute PE increased between 2012–2020 and (2) determine if any baseline characteristics are associated with ED discharge.

## METHODS

### Data Source

We conducted a serial cross-sectional analysis leveraging data from the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NHAMCS) between the years 2012–2020. NHAMCS is a nationally representative probability sample that reflects ED visits to non-federal, non-military, and non-veterans’ administrations hospitals. The NHAMCS survey is published on an annual basis by the National Center for Health Statistics at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Methods for primary data collection of the NHAMCS have been described in detail elsewhere (22,23). Briefly, the NHAMCS utilizes a three-stage probability design to formulate a representative sample of weighted patient visits to United States EDs. A sample of geographical defined areas serve as the primary sampling units where emergency service areas are identified and assigned a random four-week reporting interval to report on a random sample of ED visits. Survey completion and data reporting are conducted entirely by trained hospital personnel. Data elements collected by the NHAMCS survey vary by year, but include patient sociodemographic information, hospital information, comorbidities, vital signs (as continuous variables), physician diagnoses, clinical presentations, treatments received, diagnostics ordered, and ED dispositions. Supplemental Table S1 illustrates the NHAMCS survey codes utilized to identify the variables of interest for the present study. In this analysis, there are no missing date for age, sex, race, and ethnicity. However, several comorbidity variables including coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, alcohol use disorder, asthma, osteoporosis, depression, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea are missing in <7% of patients as these variables were not coded in the 2012–2013 surveys.

A total of 9 files of survey data were obtained and utilized for this analysis. All datasets are publicly available for use at the NCHS website (https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/ahcd/). As all data were deidentified and publicly available, Institutional Review Board approval was not required for this analysis.

### Study Population and Subgroups

Patients of all ages who presented with a diagnosis of acute PE were first identified. Visits for acute PE were identified based on any PE-related billing claims based on ICD codes on the NHAMCS survey. Table S1 illustrates the ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes which were utilized to identify patients. Claims codes utilized for this analysis were selected based on prior work (24–26). Following identification, patients were excluded if they had an unspecified disposition. Patients were censored from the analysis if they died while in the ED, died on arrival, left prior to evaluation by staff, left prior to treatment completion, left against medical advice, or were transferred to another hospital system directly from the ED.

In order to better investigate patients who were at low risk of PE-related death, subgroup analyses were performed using previously established risk stratification tools (27,28). Patients were stratified based on hemodynamic stability (defined as heart rate <110 bpm, systolic blood pressure >100 mmHg, and pulse oxygenation >90%), a low-risk pulmonary embolism severity index (PESI) class (class I or II), and a low risk simplified PESI (sPESI) score (score of 0). An overview of how these scores were calculated with the survey variables can be found in Supplemental Table S1.

### Primary Outcomes and Exposure

The primary endpoint of this analysis was the proportion of ED visits for acute PE that resulted in patient discharge directly from the ED. This variable was defined as an ED visit that did not result in hospital admission and did not have any other coded visit dispositions within the NHAMCS survey. For patients admitted to an ED observation unit, the final disposition following this placement was utilized for outcome classification. The primary exposure of this analysis was the year of ED visit. For illustrative purposes, visits were aggregated into three-year groups between 2012–2020 and visualized longitudinally with time.

### Statistical Analysis

All analyses were conducted utilizing the multistage probability survey design with the associated visit weights to obtain national estimates. Summary statistics were utilized to compare baseline characteristics. Continuous variables are reported as mean ± standard error and categorical variables as count (percentage). Baseline covariates were compared temporally utilizing standardized mean differences. All outcomes were reported as percentages (95% confidence interval). Confidence intervals were calculated by utilizing a logistic regression model to estimate a Wald-type interval.

To investigate temporal trends, survey-weighted quasi-binomial and quasi-Poisson regression models were utilized to obtain an estimate of the risk ratio with year of the visit included as a continuous linear variable. To investigate variables associated with discharge from the ED, similar survey-weighted quasi-binomial and quasi-Poisson regression models were also performed. Finally, to investigate variables associated with oral anticoagulant prescription among discharged patients, similar survey-weighted regression models were utilized. For all regression analyses, both univariable and multivariable models are reported. For all multivariable models, adjustment was made based on age, sex, race, ethnicity, and geographic region.

As this study utilized claims-based data and diagnoses were not able to be thoroughly adjudicated, we performed 2 sensitivity analyses to evaluate the reliability of the findings. First, we performed a subsequent analysis including only patients who received a CT scan in the ED. Second, we performed an analysis including only patients who had acute PE as the first coded diagnosis in the NHAMCS survey.

All statistical analyses were performed utilizing R version 4.1.0 in RStudio (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with the “survey” package for analysis. Figures were plotted utilizing Python version 3.10 (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE). Statistical significance was set at a two-tailed p-value< 0.05.

## RESULTS

### Study Population

Figure 1 depicts the flow diagram illustrating selection of the study population. Between 2012–2020, there were an estimated 1,827,207 ED visits for acute PE in the US. Among those visits, 29,523 (1.62%) were excluded as their visit resulted in an unspecified disposition. After exclusions, 1,797,684 patients remained. Of the remaining visits, 28,675 (1.57%) were censored from the analytical cohort due to death in the ED, 26,312 (1.44%) due to the patient leaving prior to treatment completion or against medical advice, and 107,397 (5.88%) due to transfer to another hospital system. In the final analytical cohort, there were a total of 1,635,300 weighted visits for acute PE during the study period.

### Baseline Characteristics of the Study Population

Table 1 depicts the baseline characteristics, hospital information, and risk stratification for patients within the study cohort stratified over time. Overall, the number of estimated ED visits for acute PE increased from 370,000 between 2012–2008 to 745,833 between 2018–2020. Among the whole cohort, the mean age was 57.7 ± 2.19, 39.1% (N=640,092) were male, 73.9% (N=1,208,183) were white, and 9.18% (N=150,188) were Hispanic or Latino. A total of 17.3% (N=283,212) of patients were treated in a teaching hospital and 7.15% (N=112,645) of patients were treated in a rural location.

Patients presenting with acute PE had high rates of comorbid cardiopulmonary disease including 21.4% (N=349,992) with COPD, 12.2% (N=199,729) with congestive heart failure, 13.8% (N=211,877) with coronary artery disease, 17.7% (N=271,481) with hyperlipidemia, and 41.6% (N=638,371) with hypertension. On average, included patients had 2.28 ± 0.23 comorbid chronic conditions. Many of the baseline comorbidities remained relatively constant over the nine-year study period including dementia, congestive heart failure, diabetes, end stage renal disease, obesity, asthma, history of HIV, and history of VTE. Rates of cancer (13.0% between 2012–2014 and 6.69% between 2018–2020) and COPD (28.3% between 2012–2014 and 18.8% between 2018–2020) decreased over time.

The most frequent clinical symptom on presentation was dyspnea occurring in 43.3% (N=707,586) of patients followed by chest pain occurring in 25.2% (N=412,549) of patients. Among vital sign abnormalities, febrile temperatures were recorded in 0.71% (N=10,697) of patients, tachycardia in 33.2% (N=508,530), hypotension in 0.43% (N=6,677), tachypnea in 33.8% (N=531,872), and oxygenation desaturation in 6.50% (N=100,908). To better understand PE severity, patients were stratified based on hemodynamic stability, PESI risk class, and sPESI scores. Among the cohort, 61.7% (N=919,292) of patients were hemodynamically stable, 62.4% (N=910,898) of patients were of PESI risk class I or II, and 44.9% (N=733,776) of patients were of sPESI score 0. Rates of hemodynamic stability (55.2% between 2012–2014 and 58.2% between 2018–2020) and PESI risk class I or II (65.6% between 2012–2014 and 61.2% between 2018–2020) remained constant over the study duration (Table 1).

### National Trends in ED Discharge Rates for Acute PE

Figure 2 illustrates the estimated rates of admission and discharge for all patients with acute PE presenting to United States EDs from 2012–2020. Overall, 30.7% (95% CI, 22.3%–41.0%) of patients with acute PE were discharged from the ED over the nine-year period. Discharge rates appeared to have remained constant over time from 38.2% (95% CI, 17.9%–64.0%) between 2012–2014 to 33.4% (95% CI, 21.0%–49.0%) between 2018–2020. Over the nine-year study duration, there was no increase in ED discharge for acute PE over time (adjusted risk ratio, 1.01 per year; 95% CI, 0.89–1.14; p=0.85) (Table 2).

Two sensitivity analyses were also performed to further validate the trends observed in the primary analysis. Among patients with a diagnosis of acute PE who also had a CT scan during their ED course, similar findings were observed with relatively constant rates of discharge over the study duration (adjusted risk ratio: 1.02 per year; 95% CI, 0.87–1.19; p=0.82) (Figure S1). Conversely, among patients with acute PE as the first coded diagnosis, there was a significant increase in the proportion of patients discharged increasing from 9.65% (95% CI, 3.25%–25.0%) between 2012–2014 to 20.6% (95% CI, 12.3%–32.0%) between 2018–2020 (adjusted risk ratio: 1.24; 95% CI, 1.06–1.47; p=0.009) (Figure S2).

### Discharge Rates Among Low-Risk PE Patients

Figure 3 depicts the temporal relationship between discharge rates of patients with PE identified as low risk. When stratified based on hemodynamic stability, rates of discharge of low-risk PE patients remained constant over the study duration (adjusted risk ratio, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.81–1.13; p=0.60) (Figure 3A).

From 2012–2020, only 35.9% (95% CI, 23.9%–50.0%) of patients with a low-risk PESI risk class and 33.1% (95% CI, 21.6%–47.0%) of patients with low-risk sPESI score were discharged from the ED setting. Among these groups, temporal trends in discharge rates remained relatively constant over the nine years investigated for both low-risk patients determined by PESI score (adjusted risk ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.84–1.18; p=0.98) and by sPESI score (adjusted risk ratio, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.85–1.27; p=0.67) (Figure 3B-C).

### Predictors of Discharge Among Patients with Acute PE

Table 2 depicts the results of the univariable and multivariable regression analysis to assess for clinical variables associated with ED discharge for acute PE. Among patients admitted, hospitalization length of stay was on average 6.31 ± 1.01 days. Among ED visits between 2012–2020, no clinical variables including any demographic information (e.g., age, sex, race), hospital features (e.g., teaching hospital status, region, rural location), or comorbidities (e.g., chronic kidney disease, congestive heart failure, COPD), were associated with ED discharge. Likewise, risk stratification frameworks including hemodynamically stable patients (adjusted risk ratio, 1.15, 95% CI, 0.65–2.04), low-risk PESI scores (adjusted risk ratio, 0.96, 95% CI, 0.43–2.13), and low-risk sPESI scores (adjusted risk ratio, 1.06 95% CI, 0.58–1.93) were not associated with ED discharge. When the cohort was sub-divided to include only patients who were hemodynamically stable, of low-risk PESI class, or of low-risk sPESI score, no demographic information or hospital features investigated were associated with ED discharge within the multivariable regression analysis (Table S2).

### Medications Prescribed During ED Encounters

Among patients admitted to the hospital following their ED encounter with medication information available, heparin products were the most frequently prescribed anticoagulant agents utilized in 68.9% (N=703,454) of patients. In admitted patients, 8.26% (N=84,336) received a factor Xa inhibitor. Among discharged patients with medication information available, the most frequently used anticoagulant class was factor Xa inhibitors utilized in 43.2% (N=102,758) of patients, of which apixaban was the most widely prescribed agent in 25.7% (N= 61,225) followed by rivaroxaban in 12.7% (N= 30,217). Among discharged patients, factor Xa inhibitors were prescribed more than three-fold more frequently at teaching hospitals (adjusted risk ratio, 3.53, 95% CI, 1.48–8.38, p=0.006). Additionally, discharged patients were more likely to receive a factor Xa inhibitor for anticoagulation if they had private insurance (adjusted risk ratio, 5.03, 95% CI, 1.50–16.9, p=0.011) and less likely if they had Medicaid insurance (adjusted risk ratio, 0.08, 95% CI, 0.011–0.061, p=0.017).

## DISCUSSION

In this nationwide study, we investigated the contemporary temporal trends in discharge rates for acute PE within United States EDs. The central finding of our analysis was that the proportion of ED visits resulting in discharge between the years 2012–2020 remained relatively unchanged in the United States, including within low-risk groups where nearly two-thirds of these visits still result in hospitalization. Importantly, we did not find any baseline patient or hospital characteristics predictive of outpatient management for acute PE; however, utilization of oral anticoagulation at discharge was more frequent at teaching institutions and among patients with private insurances.

Acute PE is a common diagnosis encountered within the ED setting, and its prevalence continues to rise within the United States (24,29,30). Previous studies have established the safety of outpatient management in both randomized and non-randomized populations and current recommendations endorse its use in appropriately triaged, low-risk patients (10). In addition, updated guidelines for management of PE, including the ESC and CHEST society documents, recommend outpatient care if certain criteria are met, such as stable hemodynamics, low risk of death based on stratification scores, and a feasible outpatient plan (10,11). Moreover, inpatient management for acute PE is expensive, with some estimates from over a decade ago suggesting a cost of nearly $9,000 per hospitalization (12,13). Prior studies have demonstrated the substantial healthcare cost saving of utilizing outpatient management for acute PE (31).

Despite the recommended changes in practice, rates of adoption of outpatient management for acute PE have been variable (32). For instance, a nationwide analysis covering the years 2007 to 2012 demonstrated a rise in the outpatient management of acute PE, from 3.9% to 6.7% (33). Similarly, in a Canadian cohort of patients, ED discharge significantly increased from 8.79% to 14.3% from 2000–2009. Nevertheless, others have found no change in the adoption of outpatient management (15,20). In a multicenter study among a small cohort of 7 community hospitals, temporal trends did not significantly increase between 2012–2018, with nearly 85% of visits resulting in admission (17).

This analysis, which leverages a longitudinal nationwide sample of ED visits, found similar trends among a larger and more contemporary timeframe. Consistent with other studies examining changes in the early 2010s, we found that rates of adoption remained largely stable over the last nine years. This plateau in adoption rates means a large proportion of patients with PE, including low risk PE, remain hospitalized for treatment despite clinical evidence and guideline recommendations suggesting otherwise. These findings were consistent in two of the three analyses performed including the primary cohort and one sensitivity analysis. Among patients with a first coded diagnosis of acute PE, we observed a small but statistically significant increase in discharge rates, although overall rates remained low consistent with the primary findings.

In our analysis, we also risk stratified patients based on previously established clinical prediction tools to identify those at low risk. Interestingly, among these low-risk populations, we found that nearly two-thirds of patients were still managed with inpatient hospitalization. In fact, when assessed temporally, rates of discharge among low-risk patients remained constant over the nine years of the analysis. The impetus for why outpatient management has plateaued remains unclear. Comorbidities did not significantly differ among those admitted or discharged with acute PE. Furthermore, additional clinical factors, such as the PE risk scores, were not predictive of outpatient care. However, we did find that patients treated at teaching hospitals and those with private insurance had higher rates of oral anticoagulant prescription at discharge, which may in part explain the observed trends. Of importance, these findings must be interpreted with caution due to the possible influence of multiple testing. Nevertheless, since accessibility to oral anticoagulation may have influenced the patterns we observed in this analysis, we speculate that increasing availability of these agents may support implementation of ED discharge for low-risk PE patients. Finally, as the decision to admit to the hospital is multifactorial, numerous other factors are also likely involved including provider discomfort with outpatient management, poor clinical systems to allow for short-term follow-up and management of these patients, and medico-legal concerns (34,35). Further research to investigate these reasons more precisely is certainly warranted.

Our study has several important limitations. First, our analysis leveraged a dataset which relied on administrative diagnostic codes for patient identification. Like other nationwide studies, this analysis may be susceptible to misclassification as the reported diagnoses were not able to be sufficiently adjudicated. Nevertheless, the billing codes utilized for this study have been extensively described in the prior literature and two sensitivity analyses were performed to further validate our findings (24–26). Second, due to the cross-sectional nature of the dataset, our analysis was only able to capture ED visits at one instance in time, limiting our ability to examine other important outcomes of interest, including recurrent VTE, bleeding and death. Third, while a strength of the NHAMCS dataset was that it was able to provide more granular patient-specific information as compared to other claims-based datasets, it was not able to fully capture a patient’s complete medical history and it was impossible to know if a single patient represented multiple ED visits. Thus, it remains possible that the estimated risk stratifications scores reported in this analysis may under-estimate the true risk associated with each patient. Moreover, right ventricular assessment, burden of thrombotic disease and other high-risk features such as pulmonary infarct were not available in this dataset. These additional risk factors have demonstrated influence on admission decisions for low risk PE patients (36). Similarly, determination of hemodynamic stability was based only on one set of vital signs which may not accurately reflect each patient’s true hemodynamic profile. Additionally, reasons for admission may be driven by non-PE reasons, such as management of comorbid conditions which may not have been captured within administrative data. Finally, this analysis included data up to 2020, which coincided with the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. Whether the onset of COVID-19 may have influenced findings in this latter period is unclear.

## CONCLUSION

In summary, we examined the real-world, national trends in discharge rates for acute PE within United States EDs over the past nine years. We demonstrate that outpatient management appears to have remained relatively unchanged since 2012, and a considerable proportion of low-risk patients are still managed with inpatient hospitalization. While no characteristics were predictive of outpatient management for acute PE, we found that utilization of oral anticoagulation at discharge was more frequent at teaching institutions and among patients with private insurances which may partially explain these trends. Altogether these findings suggest that outpatient management of acute PE remains underutilized despite clinical evidence and guideline recommendations. Further investigation into understanding the root causes of ED triage decisions and dedicated interventions to improve appropriate outpatient management utilization remain warranted.
